# Product register

When design SERVES the product: app UIs, admin dashboards, settings panels, data tables, tools, authenticated surfaces, anything where the user is in a task.

## The product slop test

Not "would someone say AI made this." Familiarity is often a feature here. The test is: would a user fluent in the category's best tools (Linear, Figma, Notion, Raycast, Stripe come to mind) sit down and trust this interface, or pause at every subtly-off component?

Product UI's failure mode isn't flatness, it's strangeness without purpose: over-decorated buttons, mismatched form controls, gratuitous motion, display fonts where labels should be, invented affordances for standard tasks. The bar is earned familiarity. The tool should disappear into the task.

## Typography

- **One family is often right.** Product UIs don't need display/body pairing. A well-tuned sans carries headings, buttons, labels, body, data.
- **Fixed rem scale, not fluid.** Clamp-sized headings don't serve product UI. Users view at consistent DPI, and a fluid h1 that shrinks in a sidebar looks worse, not better.
- **Tighter scale ratio.** 1.125–1.2 between steps is typical. More type elements here than on brand surfaces; exaggerated contrast creates noise.
- **Line length still applies for prose** (65–75ch). Data and compact UI can run denser; tables at 120ch+ are fine.

## Color

Product defaults to Restrained. A single surface can earn Committed (a dashboard where one category color carries a report, an onboarding flow with a drenched welcome screen), but Restrained is the floor.

- State-rich semantic vocabulary: hover, focus, active, disabled, selected, loading, error, warning, success, info. Standardize these.
- Accent color used for primary actions, current selection, and state indicators only, not decoration.
- A second neutral layer for sidebars, toolbars, and panels (slightly cooler or warmer than the content surface).

## Layout

- Responsive behavior is structural (collapse sidebar, responsive table, breakpoint-driven columns), not fluid typography.

## Components

Every interactive component has: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error. Don't ship with half of these.

- Skeleton states for loading, not spinners in the middle of content.
- Empty states that teach the interface, not "nothing here."
- Consistent affordances across the surface. Same button shape. Same form-control vocabulary. Same icon style.

## Motion

- 150–250 ms on most transitions. Users are in flow; don't make them wait for choreography.
- Motion conveys state, not decoration. State change, feedback, loading, reveal: nothing else.
- No orchestrated page-load sequences. Product loads into a task; users don't want to watch it load.

## Product bans (on top of the shared absolute bans)

- Decorative motion that doesn't convey state.
- Inconsistent component vocabulary across screens. If the "save" button looks different in two places, one is wrong.
- Display fonts in UI labels, buttons, data.
- Reinventing standard affordances for flavor (custom scrollbars, weird form controls, non-standard modals).
- Heavy color or full-saturation accents on inactive states.
- Modal as first thought. Modals are usually laziness. Exhaust inline / progressive alternatives first.

## Product permissions

Product can afford things brand surfaces can't.

- System fonts and familiar sans defaults (Inter, SF Pro, system-ui stacks).
- Standard navigation patterns: top bar + side nav, breadcrumbs, tabs, command palettes.
- Density. Tables with many rows, panels with many labels, dense information when users need it.
- Consistency over surprise. The same visual vocabulary screen to screen is a virtue; delight is saved for moments, not pages.

A filled-in folio field takes precedence over its collection, then the House. Leave a field blank to inherit it. Working titles belong to each folio; charter articles accumulate across the three levels.

Dossier
The brief that tells the room what a piece is for.
Charter
Required or preferred standards for your House, collection or folio.
Edition
A saved version of the dossier, with its source and reason.
Amendment
A proposed change to the dossier. It takes effect when you file it.

Open the House to arrange collections, inspect inherited context and read the register of changes. “What the models read” shows the assembled dossier and charter; individual tools add their own instructions and excerpts. The Engine room holds developer diagnostics.

When the piece changes direction: Refine the dossier yourself, or review an amendment offered in the margin. The room uses the updated brief on its next pass.

04 · At the desk

Writing in flow

The page stays central. Help can wait in the margin.

While you work, Twyne can bring comments, sources, books, records and connections to earlier writing beside the relevant passage. Hover or focus a marker to see its connections; click it to open the conversation in the same margin.

A quieter page

Automatic focus uses your typing cadence to quiet the room during a sustained run. New ambient cards wait. When you pause or reach for the room, its controls return. You can enter focus yourself or leave it with Esc.

Help when you need it

When a passage stalls, the margin can offer one relevant connection or a short way into the next sentence. These are suggestions you can set aside. A change of purpose may prompt an amendment; it never silently rewrites your dossier.

Your controls: Automatic review, margin tools, automatic focus and cover lookups have separate switches in the review controls. Timing and item preferences are learned on this device. Cover lookups send book or record titles to external catalogues.

05 · The editorial room

Your editors

Five resident voices. Each reads with a different lens. Together they cover the ground a single editor can't.

Arrange your room

Custom editors: Visit{" "} the Room of Editors {" "} to add, edit, or rearrange your cast. Each editor needs a name, a role, and a description of their voice. The AI uses these to stay in character.

Changing the Model

Each editor's voice is shaped by the model that reads for them. A careful, precise model makes Mlle. Sceptique sharper. A warmer model makes Sœur Encourageante more generous. Go to{" "} Preferences {" "} to assign different models to different tasks — the room adapts.

06 · The editorial room

The galley proof

Check the shape of the draft, then choose an editorial reading.

The static features are deterministic — sentence length distribution, type-token ratio, citation density, paragraph shape. These never call an API and never cost a token. They give you a cold, honest picture of the draft's mechanical health.

Quick check

When the signed-in service is available, the default check uses one typed judgement request to assess your enabled criteria, including custom ones. This produces a grade without separate verdicts from the five editors. If the quick check is unavailable, Twyne tries the room reading instead.

Ask the editors

Choose “Ask the editors” for the independent room reading. Each persona gives a score and rationale. That path combines editorial verdicts with static features; its Target Fit check caps shape scores when the piece misses its audience or purpose.

Grading scale:

  • A range — Publishable or nearly so. Minor polish.
  • B range — Solid draft with clear, fixable issues.
  • C range — Doing the work but needs a real pass.
  • D–F range — The important next pass is still ahead.

Use the rationale: Read the explanation beside a grade and compare it with your purpose. The rubric gives you another reading of the draft; you decide what deserves a revision.

07 · The editorial room

Margin conversations

Threaded comments alongside the draft. Your own notes, plus the editors' voices when you ask them in.

Select any passage in the manuscript and click "Add comment" to pencil a margin note. Comments are folio-scoped — they travel with the draft, not the global state. Each comment can have replies, and you can ask any editor to weigh in by clicking "Ask an editor."

Click a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve the comment there. One conversation stays in the foreground at a time; on a narrow screen, its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to close it. Unsent replies survive switching threads during this visit, but not a reload.

08 · The editorial room

Research & citations

Research, bibliography, and citation — the machinery behind the prose.

The Apparatus has three jobs: find sources, save them, and cite them. As you write, it detects DOIs, URLs, ISBNs, and author-year references automatically. You can also search for sources by query — the panel fetches a shortlist with title, author, publisher, and a snippet. Save what matters to your bibliography.

Bibliographies are formatted in your chosen style — MLA, APA, or Chicago. Switch at any time; the saved entries reformat instantly. Copy the whole bibliography to your clipboard with one click.

The full Apparatus is available at{" "} /apparatus . The right-panel citation tab shows a quick view of detected references.

09 · The editorial room

Your account & Live

A name in the room. A conversation when you need one.

Sign in with Not Organic to use your account, hosted credits and plan across devices. Your account name and picture identify you in the room; your email belongs in private account settings. You can keep writing locally without signing in.

Open Talk from the compositor, an editor’s comment or the narration player to speak with an editor. Live shows captions, lets you mute the microphone, and can find passages or propose edits. Approve a proposed edit before it changes your manuscript. Switching folios ends the conversation; captions and microphone recordings are not saved.

Live requires a Pro plan or available Twyne welcome credit. A conversation reserves up to $0.50; delegated language requests have a separate $0.05 maximum each. The voice desk shows these limits before you start.

10 · Your work

Manuscript & source tools

Structure the page, work in the source, and check the printed proof.

Automatic focus uses your typing cadence to quiet the room during a sustained run. New ambient cards wait. When you pause or reach for the room, its controls return. You can enter focus yourself or leave it with Esc.

Help when you need it

When a passage stalls, the margin can offer one relevant connection or a short way into the next sentence. These are suggestions you can set aside. A change of purpose may prompt an amendment; it never silently rewrites your dossier.

Your controls: Automatic review, margin tools, automatic focus and cover lookups have separate switches in the review controls. Timing and item preferences are learned on this device. Cover lookups send book or record titles to external catalogues.

05 · The editorial room

Your editors

Five resident voices. Each reads with a different lens. Together they cover the ground a single editor can't.

Arrange your room

Custom editors: Visit{" "} the Room of Editors {" "} to add, edit, or rearrange your cast. Each editor needs a name, a role, and a description of their voice. The AI uses these to stay in character.

Changing the Model

Each editor's voice is shaped by the model that reads for them. A careful, precise model makes Mlle. Sceptique sharper. A warmer model makes Sœur Encourageante more generous. Go to{" "} Preferences {" "} to assign different models to different tasks — the room adapts.

06 · The editorial room

The galley proof

Check the shape of the draft, then choose an editorial reading.

The static features are deterministic — sentence length distribution, type-token ratio, citation density, paragraph shape. These never call an API and never cost a token. They give you a cold, honest picture of the draft's mechanical health.

Quick check

When the signed-in service is available, the default check uses one typed judgement request to assess your enabled criteria, including custom ones. This produces a grade without separate verdicts from the five editors. If the quick check is unavailable, Twyne tries the room reading instead.

Ask the editors

Choose “Ask the editors” for the independent room reading. Each persona gives a score and rationale. That path combines editorial verdicts with static features; its Target Fit check caps shape scores when the piece misses its audience or purpose.

Grading scale:

  • A range — Publishable or nearly so. Minor polish.
  • B range — Solid draft with clear, fixable issues.
  • C range — Doing the work but needs a real pass.
  • D–F range — The important next pass is still ahead.

Use the rationale: Read the explanation beside a grade and compare it with your purpose. The rubric gives you another reading of the draft; you decide what deserves a revision.

07 · The editorial room

Margin conversations

Threaded comments alongside the draft. Your own notes, plus the editors' voices when you ask them in.

Select any passage in the manuscript and click "Add comment" to pencil a margin note. Comments are folio-scoped — they travel with the draft, not the global state. Each comment can have replies, and you can ask any editor to weigh in by clicking "Ask an editor."

Click a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve the comment there. One conversation stays in the foreground at a time; on a narrow screen, its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to close it. Unsent replies survive switching threads during this visit, but not a reload.

08 · The editorial room

Research & citations

Research, bibliography, and citation — the machinery behind the prose.

The Apparatus has three jobs: find sources, save them, and cite them. As you write, it detects DOIs, URLs, ISBNs, and author-year references automatically. You can also search for sources by query — the panel fetches a shortlist with title, author, publisher, and a snippet. Save what matters to your bibliography.

Bibliographies are formatted in your chosen style — MLA, APA, or Chicago. Switch at any time; the saved entries reformat instantly. Copy the whole bibliography to your clipboard with one click.

The full Apparatus is available at{" "} /apparatus . The right-panel citation tab shows a quick view of detected references.

09 · The editorial room

Your account & Live

A name in the room. A conversation when you need one.

Sign in with Not Organic to use your account, hosted credits and plan across devices. Your account name and picture identify you in the room; your email belongs in private account settings. You can keep writing locally without signing in.

Open Talk from the compositor, an editor’s comment or the narration player to speak with an editor. Live shows captions, lets you mute the microphone, and can find passages or propose edits. Approve a proposed edit before it changes your manuscript. Switching folios ends the conversation; captions and microphone recordings are not saved.

Live requires a Pro plan or available Twyne welcome credit. A conversation reserves up to $0.50; delegated language requests have a separate $0.05 maximum each. The voice desk shows these limits before you start.

10 · Your work

Manuscript & source tools

Structure the page, work in the source, and check the printed proof.

item.stdout:
Move through the manuscript

Type / at the start of a block to open the command menu. Use the outline to jump among headings, or drag a heading's section handle to move that section and all of its subsections in one undoable edit. Find and Replace supports whole words, case sensitivity, and regular expressions.

Tables and images

Tables support a dimension picker, captions, row and column tools, cell shading, alignment, borders, and reusable visual presets. Images can be dropped, pasted, or selected from disk; selecting an image reveals its alt text, caption, alignment, width, and upload status. Online images are stored with the folio, while deliberately offline work keeps an inline copy.

Source and proof

The Typst workspace lets you edit the source and inspect a paginated proof. Source drafts recover locally after a reload. Apply a valid draft to update the folio; if another device has changed its base, resolve that conflict before applying. An invalid draft stays available to fix.

Shape the page

Notes and equations

Inline and display equations accept LaTeX and render locally. Footnotes and endnotes can be edited beside their references, and the visible page header and footer can be edited directly in the page bands. These structures remain portable in HTML and Markdown exports.

11 · Your work

Folios, export & publishing

One piece per folio. Related pieces can share a collection.

Folios are separate documents. You might keep a main draft, scratch notes and an outline together in a collection. Switch between them from the left drawer. Each folio keeps its own word count, update time, and (optionally) its own layout settings.

Export your folio as Markdown, standalone HTML, plain text, PDF, Word, Typst source, or a full Twyne backup (JSON with brief, folios, and content). Use the File menu in the masthead.

Share a public reading view of any folio. Anyone with the link can read it; no one can edit it. Unpublish instantly.

Publish to your PDS by connecting Bluesky or another ATProto provider in the Share dialog. This publishing connection is separate from your Not Organic sign-in. Twyne files a Standard.site publication and document in your own repository, serves a verifiable public reading page, and updates the same record when you re-publish. Unpublishing removes the document from your PDS.

PDF (Typst) compiles your manuscript on this device with bundled fonts. The proof supports equations and diagrams, and reports source or asset problems before export. You can also download the .typ source. Private editorial annotations are removed from that exported copy; your saved source stays intact.

12 · Your work

Bring your own key

Choose a hosted model or connect a provider you already use.

Step 1: Add a provider. Go to{" "} Preferences {" "} and turn on "Bring Your Own Key." Add your OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google key. For other providers (Groq, Together, Rivet), use the "OpenAI-compatible" option with your base URL.

Step 2: Pick models per feature. The per-feature grid lets you choose different models for the room, rubric and other tools. Use the models available from your connected provider.

Step 3: Test the connection. Each provider card has a "Test connection" button. It sends a cheap ping and shows latency. Green means go.

Supported providers:

  • OpenAI
  • Anthropic
  • Google
  • OpenAI-compatible (Groq, Together, Rivet, local servers, …)

If a connection fails: Check the provider and key in Preferences, then test the connection again. You can keep drafting while the provider is unavailable.

13 · Your work

Privacy & your data

Your manuscript is yours. We intend to keep it that way.

API keys: Saved in your browser’s IndexedDB. Remote BYOK requests pass through Twyne’s server relay, which forwards your key and request to the selected provider. Local model endpoints stay direct.

Drafts and folios: Saved locally in your browser profile via IndexedDB. Signing out does not erase that local copy. Signing into an account with no cloud snapshot can sync the existing local work into that account. Signed-in sync provides cross-device access.

AI calls: When you BYOK, your draft text goes to the provider you chose, through the relay for remote endpoints. Hosted calls go through Convex and Not Organic. Provider processing and content-logging consent are managed in Not Organic.

Published pieces: Only what you explicitly publish becomes a public reading page. Local work remains in the browser profile; sharing and collaboration grant the access you choose through their own controls.

14 · Your work

Keyboard shortcuts

Choose the labels for your keyboard. The same shortcut registry powers this guide and the desk.

Shortcut labels

The film follows your language choice in Preferences. French readers see the French edition, including narration and on-screen text; English and other languages use the English edition. With Automatic selected, Twyne follows your browser’s language preferences.

Twyne · A writer’s reference

The Manual

From the first idea to the final proof. A guide to your writing desk, the House, and the voices in the margin. See the controls, follow a walkthrough, then try it in your own draft.

01 · At the desk

Begin a piece

Give the room a direction. Then make the page your own.

  1. Set the brief. The{" "} dossier holds your audience, purpose and the shape of the piece.
  2. Write at the desk. Your draft saves on this device. The margin makes room for feedback without taking you away.
  3. Make a revision. Follow a comment to its passage, ask an editor, or inspect the{" "} galley proof. You choose what changes.

Go to the writing desk →

02 · At the desk

The dossier

Every piece worth writing needs a brief. The dossier is Twyne's way of keeping the writer honest about what they're trying to do.

Before the room opens, we ask seven questions. They are not optional flourishes — they are the spine of the editorial conversation. When you know your audience, your goal, your tone, your constraints, and what success looks like, the editors have something to grip. Without it, even the cleverest feedback is fishing in the dark.

The seven fields:

  • Working Title — A name the room can hold onto.
  • Format — Essay, memo, chapter, dispatch, proposal…
  • Audience — Name the actual reader, not a demographic.
  • Goal — What should the piece accomplish?
  • Tone — How should it feel, not just sound?
  • Constraints — Sources to keep, jargon to avoid, anecdotes to protect.
  • Success Signal — How will you know the draft has landed?

Pro tip: You can refine the dossier at any time by clicking "Refine the dossier" in the masthead. The room picks up the new brief on the next pass.

03 · At the desk

The House & collections

A standard you set once can follow the next piece.

  1. House Your reusable audience, purpose and standards.
  2. Collection Shared context for a series of related pieces.
  3. Folio One manuscript, with its own dossier. "}} {"i":1,"status":"fulfilled","value":{"chunk_id":"7059d3","wall_time_seconds":0.00001885,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3443,"output":"

A filled-in folio field takes precedence over its collection, then the House. Leave a field blank to inherit it. Working titles belong to each folio; charter articles accumulate across the three levels.

Dossier
The brief that tells the room what a piece is for.
Charter
Required or preferred standards for your House, collection or folio.
Edition
A saved version of the dossier, with its source and reason.
Amendment
A proposed change to the dossier. It takes effect when you file it.

Open the House to arrange collections, inspect inherited context and read the register of changes. “What the models read” shows the assembled dossier and charter; individual tools add their own instructions and excerpts. The Engine room holds developer diagnostics.

When the piece changes direction: Refine the dossier yourself, or review an amendment offered in the margin. The room uses the updated brief on its next pass.

04 · At the desk

Writing in flow

The page stays central. Help can wait in the margin.

While you work, Twyne can bring comments, sources, books, records and connections to earlier writing beside the relevant passage. Hover or focus a marker to see its connections; click it to open the conversation in the same margin.

A quieter page

Automatic focus uses your typing cadence to quiet the room during a sustained run. New ambient cards wait. When you pause or reach for the room, its controls return. You can enter focus yourself or leave it with Esc.

Help when you need it

When a passage stalls, the margin can offer one relevant connection or a short way into the next sentence. These are suggestions you can set aside. A change of purpose may prompt an amendment; it never silently rewrites your dossier.

Your controls: Automatic review, margin tools, automatic focus and cover lookups have separate switches in the review controls. Timing and item preferences are learned on this device. Cover lookups send book or record titles to external catalogues.

05 · The editorial room

Your editors

Five resident voices. Each reads with a different lens. Together they cover the ground a single editor can't.

Arrange your room

Custom editors: Visit{" "} the Room of Editors {" "} to add, edit, or rearrange your cast. Each editor needs a name, a role, and a description of their voice. The AI uses these to stay in character.

Changing the Model

Each editor's voice is shaped by the model that reads for them. A careful, precise model makes Mlle. Sceptique sharper. A warmer model makes Sœur Encourageante more generous. Go to{" "} Preferences {" "} to assign different models to different tasks — the room adapts.

06 · The editorial room

The galley proof

Check the shape of the draft, then choose an editorial reading.

The static features are deterministic — sentence length distribution, type-token ratio, citation density, paragraph shape. These never call an API and never cost a token. They give you a cold, honest picture of the draft's mechanical health.

Quick check

When the signed-in service is available, the default check uses one typed judgement request to assess your enabled criteria, including custom ones. This produces a grade without separate verdicts from the five editors. If the quick check is unavailable, Twyne tries the room reading instead.

Ask the editors

Choose “Ask the editors” for the independent room reading. Each persona gives a score and rationale. That path combines editorial verdicts with static features; its Target Fit check caps shape scores when the piece misses its audience or purpose.

gives you another reading of the draft; you decide what deserves a revision.

07 · The editorial room

Margin conversations

Threaded comments alongside the draft. Your own notes, plus the editors' voices when you ask them in.

Select any passage in the manuscript and click "Add comment" to pencil a margin note. Comments are folio-scoped — they travel with the draft, not the global state. Each comment can have replies, and you can ask any editor to weigh in by clicking "Ask an editor."

Click a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve the comment there. One conversation stays in the foreground at a time; on a narrow screen, its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to close it. Unsent replies survive switching threads during this visit, but not a reload.

08 · The editorial room

Research & citations

Research, bibliography, and citation — the machinery behind the prose.

The Apparatus has three jobs: find sources, save them, and cite them. As you write, it detects DOIs, URLs, ISBNs, and author-year references automatically. You can also search for sources by query — the panel fetches a shortlist with title, author, publisher, and a snippet. Save what matters to your bibliography.

Bibliographies are formatted in your chosen style — MLA, APA, or Chicago. Switch at any time; the saved entries reformat instantly. Copy the whole bibliography to your clipboard with one click.

The full Apparatus is available at{" "} /apparatus . The right-panel citation tab shows a quick view of detected references.

09 · The editorial room

Your account & Live

A name in the room. A conversation when you need one.

Sign in with Not Organic to use your account, hosted credits and plan across devices. Your account name and picture identify you in the room; your email belongs in private account settings. You can keep writing locally without signing in.

Open Talk from the compositor, an editor’s comment or the narration player to speak with an editor. Live shows captions, lets you mute the microphone, and can find passages or propose edits. Approve a proposed edit before it changes your manuscript. Switching folios ends the conversation; captions and microphone recordings are not saved.

Live requires a Pro plan or available Twyne welcome credit. A conversation reserves up to $0.50; delegated language requests have a separate $0.05 maximum each. The voice desk shows these limits before you start.

10 · Your work

Manuscript & source tools

Structure the page, work in the source, and check the printed proof.

Move through the manuscript

Type / at the start of a block to open the command menu. Use the outline to jump among headings, or drag a heading's section handle to move that section and all of its subsections in one undoable edit. Find and Replace supports whole words, case sensitivity, and regular expressions.

Tables and images

Tables support a dimension picker, captions, row and column tools, cell shading, alignment, borders, and reusable visual presets. Images can be dropped, pasted, or selected from disk; selecting an image reveals its alt text, caption, alignment, width, and upload status. Online images are stored with the folio, while deliberately offline work keeps an inline copy.

Source and proof

The Typst workspace lets you edit the source and inspect a paginated proof. Source drafts recover locally after a reload. Apply a valid draft to update the folio; if another device has changed its base, resolve that conflict before applying. An invalid draft stays available to fix.

Shape the page

Notes and equations

Inline and display equations accept LaTeX and render locally. Footnotes and endnotes can be edited beside their references, and the visible page header and footer can be edited directly in the page bands. These structures remain portable in HTML and Markdown exports.

11 · Your work

Folios, export & publishing

One piece per folio. Related pieces can share a collection.

Folios are separate documents. You might keep a main draft, scratch notes and an outline together in a collection. Switch between them from the left drawer. Each folio keeps its own word count, update time, and (optionally) its own layout settings.

Export your folio as Markdown, standalone HTML, plain text, PDF, Word, Typst source, or a full Twyne backup (JSON with brief, folios, and content). Use the File menu in the masthead.

Share a public reading view of any folio. Anyone with the link can read it; no one can edit it. Unpublish instantly.

Publish to your PDS by connecting Bluesky or another ATProto provider in the Share dialog. This publishing connection is separate from your Not Organic sign-in. Twyne files a Standard.site publication and document in your own repository, serves a verifiable public reading page, and updates the same record when you re-publish. Unpublishing removes the document from your PDS.

PDF (Typst) compiles your manuscript on this device with bundled fonts. The proof supports equations and diagrams, and reports source or asset problems before export. You can also download the .typ source. Private editorial annotations are removed from that exported copy; your saved source stays intact.

12 · Your work

Bring your own key

Choose a hosted model or connect a provider you already use.

Step 1: Add a provider. Go to{" "} Preferences {" "} and turn on "Bring Your Own Key." Add your OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google key. For other providers (Groq, Together, Rivet), use the "OpenAI-compatible" option with your base URL.

Step 2: Pick models per feature. The per-feature grid lets you choose different models for the room, rubric and other tools. Use the models available from your connected provider.

Step 3: Test the connection. Each provider card has a "Test connection" button. It sends a cheap ping and shows latency. Green means go.

Supported providers:

  • OpenAI
  • Anthropic
  • Google
  • OpenAI-compatible (Groq, Together, Rivet, local servers, …)

If a connection fails: Check the provider and key in Preferences, then test the connection again. You can keep drafting while the provider is unavailable.

13 · Your work

Privacy & your data

Your manuscript is yours. We intend to keep it that way.

API keys: Saved in your browser’s IndexedDB. Remote BYOK requests pass through Twyne’s server relay, which forwards your key and request to the selected provider. Local model endpoints stay direct.

Drafts and folios: Saved locally in your browser profile via IndexedDB. Signing out does not erase that local copy. Signing into an account with no cloud snapshot can sync the existing local work into that account. Signed-in sync provides cross-device access.

AI calls: When you BYOK, your draft text goes to the provider you chose, through the relay for remote endpoints. Hosted calls go through Convex and Not Organic. Provider processing and content-logging consent are managed in Not Organic.

Published pieces: Only what you explicitly publish becomes a public reading page. Local work remains in the browser profile; sharing and collaboration grant the access you choose through their own controls.

14 · Your work

Keyboard shortcuts

Choose the labels for your keyboard. The same shortcut registry powers this guide and the desk.

Shortcut labels

The film follows your language choice in Preferences. French readers see the French edition, including narration and on-screen text; English and other languages use the English edition. With Automatic selected, Twyne follows your browser’s language preferences.

gives you another reading of the draft; you decide what deserves a revision.

07 · The editorial room

Margin conversations

Threaded comments alongside the draft. Your own notes, plus the editors' voices when you ask them in.

Select any passage in the manuscript and click "Add comment" to pencil a margin note. Comments are folio-scoped — they travel with the draft, not the global state. Each comment can have replies, and you can ask any editor to weigh in by clicking "Ask an editor."

Click a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve the comment there. One conversation stays in the foreground at a time; on a narrow screen, its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to close it. Unsent replies survive switching threads during this visit, but not a reload.

08 · The editorial room

Research & citations

Research, bibliography, and citation — the machinery behind the prose.

The Apparatus has three jobs: find sources, save them, and cite them. As you write, it detects DOIs, URLs, ISBNs, and author-year references automatically. You can also search for sources by query — the panel fetches a shortlist with title, author, publisher, and a snippet. Save what matters to your bibliography.

Bibliographies are formatted in your chosen style — MLA, APA, or Chicago. Switch at any time; the saved entries reformat instantly. Copy the whole bibliography to your clipboard with one click.

The full Apparatus is available at{" "} /apparatus . The right-panel citation tab shows a quick view of detected references.

09 · The editorial room

Your account & Live

A name in the room. A conversation when you need one.

Sign in with Not Organic to use your account, hosted credits and plan across devices. Your account name and picture identify you in the room; your email belongs in private account settings. You can keep writing locally without signing in.

Open Talk from the compositor, an editor’s comment or the narration player to speak with an editor. Live shows captions, lets you mute the microphone, and can find passages or propose edits. Approve a proposed edit before it changes your manuscript. Switching folios ends the conversation; captions and microphone recordings are not saved.

Live requires a Pro plan or available Twyne welcome credit. A conversation reserves up to $0.50; delegated language requests have a separate $0.05 maximum each. The voice desk shows these limits before you start.

10 · Your work

Manuscript & source tools

Structure the page, work in the source, and check the printed proof.

Move through the manuscript

Type / at the start of a block to open the command menu. Use the outline to jump among headings, or drag a heading's section handle to move that section and all of its subsections in one undoable edit. Find and Replace supports whole words, case sensitivity, and regular expressions.

Tables and images

Tables support a dimension picker, captions, row and column tools, cell shading, alignment, borders, and reusable visual presets. Images can be dropped, pasted, or selected from disk; selecting an image reveals its alt text, caption, alignment, width, and upload status. Online images are stored with the folio, while deliberately offline work keeps an inline copy.

Source and proof

The Typst workspace lets you edit the source and inspect a paginated proof. Source drafts recover locally after a reload. Apply a valid draft to update the folio; if another device has changed its base, resolve that conflict before applying. An invalid draft stays available to fix.

Shape the page

Notes and equations

Inline and display equations accept LaTeX and render locally. Footnotes and endnotes can be edited beside their references, and the visible page header and footer can be edited directly in the page bands. These structures remain portable in HTML and Markdown exports.

11 · Your work

Folios, export & publishing

One piece per folio. Related pieces can share a collection.

Folios are separate documents. You might keep a main draft, scratch notes and an outline together in a collection. Switch between them from the left drawer. Each folio keeps its own word count, update time, and (optionally) its own layout settings.

Export your folio as Markdown, standalone HTML, plain text, PDF, Word, Typst source, or a full Twyne backup (JSON with brief, folios, and content). Use the File menu in the masthead.

Share a public reading view of any folio. Anyone with the link can read it; no one can edit it. Unpublish instantly.

Publish to your PDS by connecting Bluesky or another ATProto provider in the Share dialog. This publishing connection is separate from your Not Organic sign-in. Twyne files a Standard.site publication and document in your own repository, serves a verifiable public reading page, and updates the same record when you re-publish. Unpublishing removes the document from your PDS.

PDF (Typst) compiles your manuscript on this device with bundled fonts. The proof supports equations and diagrams, and reports source or asset problems before export. You can also download the .typ source. Private editorial annotations are removed from that exported copy; your saved source stays intact.

12 · Your work

Bring your own key

Choose a hosted model or connect a provider you already use.

Step 1: Add a provider. Go to{" "} Preferences {" "} and turn on "Bring Your Own Key." Add your OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google key. For other providers (Groq, Together, Rivet), use the "OpenAI-compatible" option with your base URL.

Step 2: Pick models per feature. The per-feature grid lets you choose different models for the room, rubric and other tools. Use the models available from your connected provider.

Step 3: Test the connection. Each provider card has a "Test connection" button. It sends a cheap ping and shows latency. Green means go.

Supported providers:

  • OpenAI
  • Anthropic
  • Google
  • OpenAI-compatible (Groq, Together, Rivet, local servers, …)

If a connection fails: Check the provider and key in Preferences, then test the connection again. You can keep drafting while the provider is unavailable.

13 · Your work

Privacy & your data

Your manuscript is yours. We intend to keep it that way.

API keys: Saved in your browser’s IndexedDB. Remote BYOK requests pass through Twyne’s server relay, which forwards your key and request to the selected provider. Local model endpoints stay direct.

Drafts and folios: Saved locally in your browser profile via IndexedDB. Signing out does not erase that local copy. Signing into an account with no cloud snapshot can sync the existing local work into that account. Signed-in sync provides cross-device access.

AI calls: When you BYOK, your draft text goes to the provider you chose, through the relay for remote endpoints. Hosted calls go through Convex and Not Organic. Provider processing and content-logging consent are managed in Not Organic.

Published pieces: Only what you explicitly publish becomes a public reading page. Local work remains in the browser profile; sharing and collaboration grant the access you choose through their own controls.

14 · Your work

Keyboard shortcuts

            <section id="marginalia" class="manual-section">
              <p class="manual-chapter">07 · The editorial room</p>
              <h2 class="manual-h2">Margin conversations</h2>
              <p class="manual-lead">
                Threaded comments alongside the draft. Your own notes, plus the
                editors' voices when you ask them in.
              </p>
              <ChapterIllustrations chapter="marginalia" />
              <p class="manual-p">
                Select any passage in the manuscript and click "Add comment" to
                pencil a margin note. Comments are folio-scoped — they travel
                with the draft, not the global state. Each comment can have
                replies, and you can ask any editor to weigh in by clicking "Ask
                an editor."
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                Click a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the
                manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve the comment there.
                One conversation stays in the foreground at a time; on a narrow
                screen, its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to
                close it. Unsent replies survive switching threads during this
                visit, but not a reload.
              </p>
            </section>
            <section id="apparatus" class="manual-section">
              <p class="manual-chapter">08 · The editorial room</p>
              <h2 class="manual-h2">Research & citations</h2>
              <p class="manual-lead">
                Research, bibliography, and citation — the machinery behind the
                prose.
              </p>
              <ChapterIllustrations chapter="apparatus" />
              <p class="manual-p">
                The Apparatus has three jobs: find sources, save them, and cite
                them. As you write, it detects DOIs, URLs, ISBNs, and
                author-year references automatically. You can also search for
                sources by query — the panel fetches a shortlist with title,
                author, publisher, and a snippet. Save what matters to your
                bibliography.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                Bibliographies are formatted in your chosen style — MLA, APA, or
                Chicago. Switch at any time; the saved entries reformat
                instantly. Copy the whole bibliography to your clipboard with
                one click.
              </p>
              <div class="manual-callout">
                <p>
                  The full Apparatus is available at{" "}
                  <Link
                    href="/apparatus"
                    class="underline hover:text-[var(--color-vermilion)]"
                  >
                    /apparatus
                  </Link>
                  . The right-panel citation tab shows a quick view of detected
                  references.
                </p>
              </div>
            </section>
            <section id="account-and-live" class="manual-section">
              <p class="manual-chapter">09 · The editorial room</p>
              <h2 class="manual-h2">Your account & Live</h2>
              <p class="manual-lead">
                A name in the room. A conversation when you need one.
              </p>
              <ChapterIllustrations chapter="account-and-live" />
              <p class="manual-p">
                Sign in with Not Organic to use your account, hosted credits and
                plan across devices. Your account name and picture identify you
                in the room; your email belongs in private account settings. You
                can keep writing locally without signing in.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                Open Talk from the compositor, an editor’s comment or the
                narration player to speak with an editor. Live shows captions,
                lets you mute the microphone, and can find passages or propose
                edits. Approve a proposed edit before it changes your
                manuscript. Switching folios ends the conversation; captions and
                microphone recordings are not saved.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                Live requires a Pro plan or available Twyne welcome credit. A
                conversation reserves up to $0.50; delegated language requests
                have a separate $0.05 maximum each. The voice desk shows these
                limits before you start.
              </p>
            </section>
            <section id="manuscript-tools" class="manual-section">
              <p class="manual-chapter">10 · Your work</p>
              <h2 class="manual-h2">Manuscript & source tools</h2>
              <p class="manual-lead">
                Structure the page, work in the source, and check the printed
                proof.
              </p>
              <ManualVideo film={MANUAL_FILMS["manuscript-tools"]} />
              <h3 class="manual-h3" id="outline-and-find">
                Move through the manuscript
              </h3>
              <ChapterIllustrations chapter="outline-and-find" />
              <p class="manual-p">
                Type <strong>/</strong> at the start of a block to open the
                command menu. Use the outline to jump among headings, or drag a
                heading's section handle to move that section and all of its
                subsections in one undoable edit. Find and Replace supports
                whole words, case sensitivity, and regular expressions.
              </p>
              <h3 class="manual-h3" id="tables-and-images">
                Tables and images
              </h3>
              <ChapterIllustrations chapter="tables-and-images" />
              <p class="manual-p">
                Tables support a dimension picker, captions, row and column
                tools, cell shading, alignment, borders, and reusable visual
                presets. Images can be dropped, pasted, or selected from disk;
                selecting an image reveals its alt text, caption, alignment,
                width, and upload status. Online images are stored with the
                folio, while deliberately offline work keeps an inline copy.
              </p>
              <h3 class="manual-h3" id="source-and-proof">
                Source and proof
              </h3>
              <ManualWalkthrough
                id="manuscript-tools"
                guide={GUIDES["manuscript-tools"]}
              />
              <p class="manual-p">
                The Typst workspace lets you edit the source and inspect a
                paginated proof. Source drafts recover locally after a reload.
                Apply a valid draft to update the folio; if another device has
                changed its base, resolve that conflict before applying. An
                invalid draft stays available to fix.
              </p>
              <h3 class="manual-h3" id="page-layout">
                Shape the page
              </h3>
              <ChapterIllustrations chapter="page-layout" />
              <h3 class="manual-h3" id="notes-and-equations">
                Notes and equations
              </h3>
              <ChapterIllustrations chapter="notes-and-equations" />
              <p class="manual-p">
                Inline and display equations accept LaTeX and render locally.
                Footnotes and endnotes can be edited beside their references,
                and the visible page header and footer can be edited directly in
                the page bands. These structures remain portable in HTML and
                Markdown exports.
              </p>
            </section>
            <section id="folios" class="manual-section">
              <p class="manual-chapter">11 · Your work</p>
              <h2 class="manual-h2">Folios, export & publishing</h2>
              <p class="manual-lead">
                One piece per folio. Related pieces can share a collection.
              </p>
              <ChapterIllustrations chapter="folios" />
              <p class="manual-p">
                Folios are separate documents. You might keep a main draft,
                scratch notes and an outline together in a collection. Switch
                between them from the left drawer. Each folio keeps its own word
                count, update time, and (optionally) its own layout settings.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>Export</strong> your folio as Markdown, standalone HTML,
                plain text, PDF, Word, Typst source, or a full Twyne backup
                (JSON with brief, folios, and content). Use the File menu in the
                masthead.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>Share</strong> a public reading view of any folio.
                Anyone with the link can read it; no one can edit it. Unpublish
                instantly.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>Publish to your PDS</strong> by connecting Bluesky or
                another ATProto provider in the Share dialog. This publishing
                connection is separate from your Not Organic sign-in. Twyne
                files a Standard.site publication and document in your own
                repository, serves a verifiable public reading page, and updates
                the same record when you re-publish. Unpublishing removes the
                document from your PDS.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>PDF (Typst)</strong> compiles your manuscript on this
                device with bundled fonts. The proof supports equations and
                diagrams, and reports source or asset problems before export.
                You can also download the .typ source. Private editorial
                annotations are removed from that exported copy; your saved
                source stays intact.
              </p>
            </section>
            <section id="byok" class="manual-section">
              <p class="manual-chapter">12 · Your work</p>
              <h2 class="manual-h2">Bring your own key</h2>
              <p class="manual-lead">
                Choose a hosted model or connect a provider you already use.
              </p>
              <ChapterIllustrations chapter="byok" />
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>Step 1: Add a provider.</strong> Go to{" "}
                <Link
                  href="/settings"
                  class="underline hover:text-[var(--color-vermilion)]"
                >
                  Preferences
                </Link>{" "}
                and turn on "Bring Your Own Key." Add your OpenAI, Anthropic, or
                Google key. For other providers (Groq, Together, Rivet), use the
                "OpenAI-compatible" option with your base URL.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>Step 2: Pick models per feature.</strong> The
                per-feature grid lets you choose different models for the room,
                rubric and other tools. Use the models available from your
                connected provider.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>Step 3: Test the connection.</strong> Each provider card
                has a "Test connection" button. It sends a cheap ping and shows
                latency. Green means go.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">Supported providers:</p>
              <ul class="manual-ul">
                <li>OpenAI</li>
                <li>Anthropic</li>
                <li>Google</li>
                <li>
                  OpenAI-compatible (Groq, Together, Rivet, local servers, …)
                </li>
              </ul>
              <div class="manual-callout">
                <p>
                  <strong>If a connection fails:</strong> Check the provider and
                  key in Preferences, then test the connection again. You can
                  keep drafting while the provider is unavailable.
                </p>
              </div>
            </section>
            <section id="privacy" class="manual-section">
              <p class="manual-chapter">13 · Your work</p>
              <h2 class="manual-h2">Privacy & your data</h2>
              <p class="manual-lead">
                Your manuscript is yours. We intend to keep it that way.
              </p>
              <ChapterIllustrations chapter="privacy" />
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>API keys:</strong> Saved in your browser’s IndexedDB.
                Remote BYOK requests pass through Twyne’s server relay, which
                forwards your key and request to the selected provider. Local
                model endpoints stay direct.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>Drafts and folios:</strong> Saved locally in your
                browser profile via IndexedDB. Signing out does not erase that
                local copy. Signing into an account with no cloud snapshot can
                sync the existing local work into that account. Signed-in sync
                provides cross-device access.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>AI calls:</strong> When you BYOK, your draft text goes
                to the provider you chose, through the relay for remote
                endpoints. Hosted calls go through Convex and Not Organic.
                Provider processing and content-logging consent are managed in
                Not Organic.
              </p>
              <p class="manual-p">
                <strong>Published pieces:</strong> Only what you explicitly
                publish becomes a public reading page. Local work remains in the
                browser profile; sharing and collaboration grant the access you
                choose through their own controls.
              </p>
            </section>
            <section id="shortcuts" class="manual-section">
              <p class="manual-chapter">14 · Your work</p>
              <h2 class="manual-h2">Keyboard shortcuts</h2>
              <p class="manual-p">
                Choose the labels for your keyboard. The same shortcut registry
                powers this guide and the desk.
              </p>
              <fieldset class="manual-platform">
                <legend>Shortcut labels</legend>
                <label>
                  <input
                    type="radio"
                    name="shortcut-platform"
                    value="mac"
                    checked={platform.value === "mac"}
                    onChange$={() => (platform.value = "mac")}
                  />
                  macOS
                </label>
                <label>
                  <input
                    type="radio"
                    name="shortcut-platform"
                    value="windows"
                    checked={platform.value === "windows"}
                    onChange$={() => (platform.value = "windows")}
                  />
                  Windows / Linux
                </label>
              </fieldset>
              <div class="manual-shortcuts">
                <KeybindingList entries={shortcuts.value} />
              </div>
            </section>
            <section id="launch-film" class="manual-section">
              <LaunchFilm />
              <p class="manual-p mt-5">
                The film follows your language choice in Preferences. French
                readers see the French edition, including narration and
                on-screen text; English and other languages use the English
                edition. With Automatic selected, Twyne follows your browser’s
                language preferences.
              </p>
            </section>
            <footer class="manual-colophon">
              <span>Twyne · The editorial room</span>
              <a href="#manual-top">Back to the beginning ↑</a>
            </footer>
          </article>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  );

Twyne · A writer’s reference

149

The Manual

150

151 From the first idea to the final proof. A guide to your writing 152 desk, the House, and the voices in the margin. See the controls, 153 follow a walkthrough, then try it in your own draft. 154

155

In this guide

01 · At the desk

181

Begin a piece

182

183 Give the room a direction. Then make the page your own. 184

185 186
    187
  1. 188 Set the brief. The{" "} 189 dossier holds your audience, purpose 190 and the shape of the piece. 191
    2. 192
  2. 193 Write at the desk. Your draft saves on this 194 device. 195 The margin makes room for feedback 196 without taking you away. 197
    3. 198
  3. 199 Make a revision. Follow a comment to its 200 passage, ask an editor, or inspect the{" "} 201 galley proof. You choose what changes. 202
    4. 203
204

205 Go to the writing desk → 206

207
208
209

02 · At the desk

210

The dossier

211

212 Every piece worth writing needs a brief. The dossier is Twyne's 213 way of keeping the writer honest about what they're trying to 214 do. 215

216 217

218 Before the room opens, we ask seven questions. They are not 219 optional flourishes — they are the spine of the editorial 220 conversation. When you know your audience, your goal, your tone, 221 your constraints, and what success looks like, the editors have 222 something to grip. Without it, even the cleverest feedback is 223 fishing in the dark. 224

225

The seven fields:

226
    227
  • 228 Working Title — A name the room can hold 229 onto. 230
    • 231
  • 232 Format — Essay, memo, chapter, dispatch, 233 proposal… 234
    • 235
  • 236 Audience — Name the actual reader, not a 237 demographic. 238
    • 239
  • 240 Goal — What should the piece accomplish? 241
    • 242
  • 243 Tone — How should it feel, not just sound? 244
    • 245
  • 246 Constraints — Sources to keep, jargon to 247 avoid, anecdotes to protect. 248
    • 249
  • 250 Success Signal — How will you know the draft 251 has landed? 252
    • 253
254
255

256 Pro tip: You can refine the dossier at any 257 time by clicking "Refine the dossier" in the masthead. The 258 room picks up the new brief on the next pass. 259

260
261
262
263

03 · At the desk

264

The House & collections

265

266 A standard you set once can follow the next piece. 267

268 269
    270
  1. 271 House 272 Your reusable audience, purpose and standards. 273
    2. 274
  2. 275 Collection 276 Shared context for a series of related pieces. 277
    3. 278
  3. 279 Folio 280 One manuscript, with its own dossier. 281
    4. 282
283

284 A filled-in folio field takes precedence over its collection, 285 then the House. Leave a field blank to inherit it. Working 286 titles belong to each folio; charter articles accumulate across 287 the three levels. 288

289
290
291
Dossier
292
The brief that tells the room what a piece is for.
293
294
295
Charter
296
297 Required or preferred standards for your House, collection 298 or folio. 299
300
301
302
Edition
303
304 A saved version of the dossier, with its source and reason. 305
306
307
308
Amendment
309
310 A proposed change to the dossier. It takes effect when you 311 file it. 312
313
314
315

316 Open the House to arrange 317 collections, inspect inherited context and read the register of 318 changes. “What the models read” shows the assembled dossier and 319 charter; individual tools add their own instructions and 320 excerpts. The Engine room holds developer diagnostics. 321

322
323

324 When the piece changes direction: Refine the 325 dossier yourself, or review an amendment offered in the 326 margin. The room uses the updated brief on its next pass. 327

328
329
330
331

04 · At the desk

332

Writing in flow

333

334 The page stays central. Help can wait in the margin. 335

336 337

338 While you work, Twyne can bring comments, sources, books, 339 records and connections to earlier writing beside the relevant 340 passage. Hover or focus a marker to see its connections; click 341 it to open the conversation in the same margin. 342

343

A quieter page

344

345 Automatic focus uses your typing cadence to quiet the room 346 during a sustained run. New ambient cards wait. When you pause 347 or reach for the room, its controls return. You can enter focus 348 yourself or leave it with Esc. 349

350

Help when you need it

351

352 When a passage stalls, the margin can offer one relevant 353 connection or a short way into the next sentence. These are 354 suggestions you can set aside. A change of purpose may prompt an 355 amendment; it never silently rewrites your dossier. 356

357
358

359 Your controls: Automatic review, margin 360 tools, automatic focus and cover lookups have separate 361 switches in the review controls. Timing and item preferences 362 are learned on this device. Cover lookups send book or record 363 titles to external catalogues. 364

365
366
367
368

07 · The editorial room

467

Margin conversations

468

469 Threaded comments alongside the draft. Your own notes, plus the 470 editors' voices when you ask them in. 471

472 473

474 Select any passage in the manuscript and click "Add comment" to 475 pencil a margin note. Comments are folio-scoped — they travel 476 with the draft, not the global state. Each comment can have 477 replies, and you can ask any editor to weigh in by clicking "Ask 478 an editor." 479

480

481 Click a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the 482 manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve the comment there. 483 One conversation stays in the foreground at a time; on a narrow 484 screen, its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to 485 close it. Unsent replies survive switching threads during this 486 visit, but not a reload. 487

488
489
490

08 · The editorial room

491

Research & citations

492

493 Research, bibliography, and citation — the machinery behind the 494 prose. 495

496 497

498 The Apparatus has three jobs: find sources, save them, and cite 499 them. As you write, it detects DOIs, URLs, ISBNs, and 500 author-year references automatically. You can also search for 501 sources by query — the panel fetches a shortlist with title, 502 author, publisher, and a snippet. Save what matters to your 503 bibliography. 504

505

506 Bibliographies are formatted in your chosen style — MLA, APA, or 507 Chicago. Switch at any time; the saved entries reformat 508 instantly. Copy the whole bibliography to your clipboard with 509 one click. 510

511
512

513 The full Apparatus is available at{" "} 514 518 /apparatus 519 520 . The right-panel citation tab shows a quick view of detected 521 references. 522

523
524
525
526

09 · The editorial room

527

Your account & Live

528

529 A name in the room. A conversation when you need one. 530

531 532

533 Sign in with Not Organic to use your account, hosted credits and 534 plan across devices. Your account name and picture identify you 535 in the room; your email belongs in private account settings. You 536 can keep writing locally without signing in. 537

538

539 Open Talk from the compositor, an editor’s comment or the 540 narration player to speak with an editor. Live shows captions, 541 lets you mute the microphone, and can find passages or propose 542 edits. Approve a proposed edit before it changes your 543 manuscript. Switching folios ends the conversation; captions and 544 microphone recordings are not saved. 545

546

547 Live requires a Pro plan or available Twyne welcome credit. A 548 conversation reserves up to $0.50; delegated language requests 549 have a separate $0.05 maximum each. The voice desk shows these 550 limits before you start. 551

552
553
554

10 · Your work

555

Manuscript & source tools

556

557 Structure the page, work in the source, and check the printed 558 proof. 559

560 561

562 Move through the manuscript 563

564 565

566 Type / at the start of a block to open the 567 command menu. Use the outline to jump among headings, or drag a 568 heading's section handle to move that section and all of its 569 subsections in one undoable edit. Find and Replace supports 570 whole words, case sensitivity, and regular expressions. 571

572

573 Tables and images 574

575 576

577 Tables support a dimension picker, captions, row and column 578 tools, cell shading, alignment, borders, and reusable visual 579 presets. Images can be dropped, pasted, or selected from disk; 580 selecting an image reveals its alt text, caption, alignment, 581 width, and upload status. Online images are stored with the 582 folio, while deliberately offline work keeps an inline copy. 583

584

585 Source and proof 586

587 591

592 The Typst workspace lets you edit the source and inspect a 593 paginated proof. Source drafts recover locally after a reload. 594 Apply a valid draft to update the folio; if another device has 595 changed its base, resolve that conflict before applying. An 596 invalid draft stays available to fix. 597

598

599 Shape the page 600

601 602

603 Notes and equations 604

605 606

607 Inline and display equations accept LaTeX and render locally. 608 Footnotes and endnotes can be edited beside their references, 609 and the visible page header and footer can be edited directly in 610 the page bands. These structures remain portable in HTML and 611 Markdown exports. 612

613
614
615

11 · Your work

616

Folios, export & publishing

617

618 One piece per folio. Related pieces can share a collection. 619

620 621

622 Folios are separate documents. You might keep a main draft, 623 scratch notes and an outline together in a collection. Switch 624 between them from the left drawer. Each folio keeps its own word 625 count, update time, and (optionally) its own layout settings. 626

627

628 Export your folio as Markdown, standalone HTML, 629 plain text, PDF, Word, Typst source, or a full Twyne backup 630 (JSON with brief, folios, and content). Use the File menu in the 631 masthead. 632

633

634 Share a public reading view of any folio. 635 Anyone with the link can read it; no one can edit it. Unpublish 636 instantly. 637

638

639 Publish to your PDS by connecting Bluesky or 640 another ATProto provider in the Share dialog. This publishing 641 connection is separate from your Not Organic sign-in. Twyne 642 files a Standard.site publication and document in your own 643 repository, serves a verifiable public reading page, and updates 644 the same record when you re-publish. Unpublishing removes the 645 document from your PDS. 646

647

648 PDF (Typst) compiles your manuscript on this 649 device with bundled fonts. The proof supports equations and 650 diagrams, and reports source or asset problems before export. 651 You can also download the .typ source. Private editorial 652 annotations are removed from that exported copy; your saved 653 source stays intact. 654

655
656
657

12 · Your work

658

Bring your own key

659

660 Choose a hosted model or connect a provider you already use. 661

662 663

664 Step 1: Add a provider. Go to{" "} 665 669 Preferences 670 {" "} 671 and turn on "Bring Your Own Key." Add your OpenAI, Anthropic, or 672 Google key. For other providers (Groq, Together, Rivet), use the 673 "OpenAI-compatible" option with your base URL. 674

675

676 Step 2: Pick models per feature. The 677 per-feature grid lets you choose different models for the room, 678 rubric and other tools. Use the models available from your 679 connected provider. 680

681

682 Step 3: Test the connection. Each provider card 683 has a "Test connection" button. It sends a cheap ping and shows 684 latency. Green means go. 685

686

Supported providers:

687
    688
  • OpenAI
    • 689
  • Anthropic
    • 690
  • Google
    • 691
  • 692 OpenAI-compatible (Groq, Together, Rivet, local servers, …) 693
    • 694
695
696

697 If a connection fails: Check the provider and 698 key in Preferences, then test the connection again. You can 699 keep drafting while the provider is unavailable. 700

701
702
703
704

13 · Your work

705

Privacy & your data

706

707 Your manuscript is yours. We intend to keep it that way. 708

709 710

711 API keys: Saved in your browser’s IndexedDB. 712 Remote BYOK requests pass through Twyne’s server relay, which 713 forwards your key and request to the selected provider. Local 714 model endpoints stay direct. 715

716

717 Drafts and folios: Saved locally in your 718 browser profile via IndexedDB. Signing out does not erase that 719 local copy. Signing into an account with no cloud snapshot can 720 sync the existing local work into that account. Signed-in sync 721 provides cross-device access. 722

723

724 AI calls: When you BYOK, your draft text goes 725 to the provider you chose, through the relay for remote 726 endpoints. Hosted calls go through Convex and Not Organic. 727 Provider processing and content-logging consent are managed in 728 Not Organic. 729

730

731 Published pieces: Only what you explicitly 732 publish becomes a public reading page. Local work remains in the 733 browser profile; sharing and collaboration grant the access you 734 choose through their own controls. 735

736
737
738

14 · Your work

739

Keyboard shortcuts

740

741 Choose the labels for your keyboard. The same shortcut registry 742 powers this guide and the desk. 743

744
745 Shortcut labels 746 756 766
767
768 769
770
771
772 773

774 The film follows your language choice in Preferences. French 775 readers see the French edition, including narration and 776 on-screen text; English and other languages use the English 777 edition. With Automatic selected, Twyne follows your browser’s 778 language preferences. 779

TWYNE · A WRITER’S REF ERENCE



The Manual
From the first idea to the final proof. A guide to your writing desk,
the House, and the voices in the margin. See the controls, follow a
walkthrough, then try it in your own draft.




01 · AT THE DESK

Begin a piece
Give the room a direction. Then make the page your own.



AT THE DESK · A VISUAL WALKTHROUGH

Find your way around the desk
Keep the dossier beside the manuscript, then handle each editorial mark where it belongs.




Illustrated with a sample draft and staged editorial feedback.


                                                                                     Click-to-Source: Alt
 Write with the dossier beside you. Open the drawer at the upper left to see the current dossier and
switch folios. Write is the editable manuscript; Home holds type, heading, and list controls.

Open a note at its passage. Select an underlined note or its coloured dot to see the quoted passage and
the editor's reasoning. Write a Reply to continue the conversation, or Strike once you've addressed the
note.

Decide on a proposed edit. Select a proposed edit's dot to compare the current words with the
replacement. Accept & stamp applies the change; Strike keeps your original wording. Close the card to
leave the decision open.


 1. Set the brief. The dossier holds your audience, purpose and the shape of the piece.

 2. Write at the desk. Your draft saves on this device. The margin makes room for feedback without taking
    you away.

 3. Make a revision. Follow a comment to its passage, ask an editor, or inspect the galley proof. You choose
    what changes.

Go to the writing desk →




02 · AT THE DESK

The dossier
Every piece worth writing needs a brief. The dossier is Twyne's way of keeping the writer honest about
what they're trying to do.



AT THE DESK · A VISUAL WALKTHROUGH

File the intent, then refine it
Give the room a reader, an aim, and useful material to work from. Revisit those choices as the piece develops.




                                                                                       Click-to-Source: Alt
 Begin with a working title. Name the piece, then use Next or the numbered sections along the foot of the
sheet. The working copy on the left shows the dossier taking shape.

Say what the piece should accomplish. Describe the change you want in the reader. The Goal box updates
in the working copy as you type; select another section to set the audience, tone, constraints, or success
signal.

Attach material with a purpose. Choose Document or Link, give it a title, and explain why it matters. Add
to dossier adds it to the working copy; Send to press files the answers and attached references.

Refile a changed brief. Choose Refine dossier at the desk and select the answer to change. Send to press
files a new edition; Back to desk leaves the current filed copy in place.


Before the room opens, we ask seven questions. They are not optional flourishes — they are the spine of
the editorial conversation. When you know your audience, your goal, your tone, your constraints, and
what success looks like, the editors have something to grip. Without it, even the cleverest feedback is
fishing in the dark.

The seven fields:

    Working Title — A name the room can hold onto.                                Click-to-Source: Alt
     Format — Essay, memo, chapter, dispatch, proposal…
